cards.title: The missing link
cards.author: Dr Niaz Murtaza
cards.why: This article is crucial for understanding debates on governance, federalism, and the importance of local government in Pakistan.
cards.summary: The author argues that the push for creating new provinces is a flawed solution to Pakistan's problems. He suggests that rulers advocating for more provinces are avoiding the proven benefits of strengthening local bodies. Local bodies are essential for bringing power closer to the people but are often absent or too weak in many parts of Pakistan.
key_facts: The idea of making many provinces is presented as a 'cure for our many ills' in Pakistan.
Afghanistan, a unitary state, has 34 units that lack legislative powers and elected bodies.
France, also a unitary state, has 18 units which lack legislative powers.
Pakistan has over 150 districts, which legally should have elected local bodies.
Local bodies are currently absent in Gilgit-Baltistan, Quetta, Punjab, Islamabad, and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa due to emergency rule.

vocab.meaning: a strong and clear request or demand for action
a state governed as a single power where the central government is supreme
a series of events where one causes the next

text: RULERS who don’t bring power closer to people via strong local bodies want us to believe that they will now bring power closer to people via more provinces. So, the false idea of making many provinces as a cure for our many ills is back with a bang.
Months after it first emerged , the bang is still more noise than a clarion call of reason. I have seen three key reports against it, but none in its favour.

Support — strong on rhetoric but weak on evidence — comes mainly from ministers and friendly analysts. One minister cites Afghanistan’s 34 units. That’s odd as Afghanistan helps us avoid the blushes of being last in South Asia on key governance metrics. It’s a unitary state whose units lack legislative powers and elected bodies. We have 150-plus stronger units (districts) which have elected bodies, at least as per the law.

Some cite unitary France’s 18 units. They too lack legislative powers. Counting them is easier than proving they cause its progress. It has democracy and civilian sway, unlike us. These key parts of the causal chain are not cited in our French politics lessons.

Rulers also ignore the proven merits of local bodies. These offer no instant cure. But with higher democracy and civilian sway present, they bring power closer to people globally. And when the two aren’t in place, nothing usually does that. But they remain our missing link between power and the powerless.

Most of us don’t have elected local bodies, they being absent in Gilgit-Baltistan, Quetta, Punjab and Islamabad and now KP due to emergency rule. Even when and where they exist, they are too weak to fix problems.

Provinces often delay their elections for long but dissolve them early. Elections are often held on non-party basis; local officials often lack a public mandate, as in Punjab, and seats for weak groups are often hogged by elites. Citizens have little say in what they do, little recourse when they fail and little voice in how they spend money. Uneven council sizes and missing tiers weaken them further. Local tasks are split among local bodies and many higher-level agencies. Local heads often lack effective control as vague supervisory powers allow interference from above. Weak coordination and capacity gaps further hamper them. Such split and bureaucratic control is high in Islamabad, Sindh and Punjab.
The setups closest to the people have the least powers.

Provinces first make voters wait for local bodies. They later make local bodies wait for cash. They only spend about five per cent of our total state funds, much lower than in many similar states. They depend heavily on provincial funds and can’t legally and practically collect much cash locally. For example, over 95pc of their funds come from such transfers in Sindh. It is often hard to see how provinces divide money across districts, but easy to see that favoured districts get more cash per head.

So, the setups closest to the people have the least powers. Would rulers who have kept local bodies so weak for so long empower new provinces? Their new capitals may be closer, but still out of reach of the masses.

The aim behind dividing provinces may be to make them powerless like local bodies and actually move power away from the people. What provinces have done to local bodies, the centre may now do to the provinces. So, the masses will have one more government level between them and real power.

Deep divisions within a setup held together tightly by its strong fear of PTI and its weak mandate make the division of provinces dicey. Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari’s diatribes exposing its electoral misdeeds and warning against forcing matters via a referendum emitted shockwaves. Our new troi­­ka — the president, prime minister and interior minister — representing all key parts of the hybrid regime, soon agreed on talks. Perhaps those fond of force have shelved it, for now.

The PPP was largely mum when judges, the opposition and activists faced abuses. It has reacted strongly, now that it’s at the receiving end of the stick. Even though it opposes the idea for the wrong reason — the fear of losing the golden goose of Karachi — the right reasons do exist.

PML-N supports this latest demand of powerful quarters via ministers, but the Sharifs stay mum. Perhaps it wants strong promises of extended patronage before giving top-level support. But it, too, may be forced to speak up when it eventually faces problems.

While our hybrid rulers continue to play self-serving games, a nuclear-armed state of nearly 250 million inches closer to multifaceted crises given their misrule. Uninterrupted democracy and civilian sway are the only way to avoid doom.
The writer has a PhD degree in political economy from the University of California, Berkeley, and 25 years of grassroots to senior-level experience across 50 countries.

cards.title: Absenteeism woes
cards.author: Parvez Rahim
cards.why: This article is vital for understanding labor market challenges, productivity concerns, and human resource management issues in Pakistan's economy.
cards.summary: Employee absenteeism is a major challenge for businesses in Pakistan, impacting productivity despite generous leave policies. Statutory requirements include 14 annual, 10 casual, and 16 sick leave days, plus festival holidays. This adds up to approximately 165 non-working days, leaving only about 200 working days annually. Reasons for absence range from feigned sickness to social, economic, personal issues, and stressful work environments.
key_facts: Top Pakistani companies historically employed highly sought-after technicians and operators.
Progressive companies often provide two weekly rest days and 20 to 25 days of annual leave.
The statutory annual leave requirement in Pakistan is 14 days per annum.
The law provides 10 days of casual leave and 16 days of sick leave annually.
Total leaves and holidays can sum up to approximately 165 days, leaving only around 200 working days in a year.
text: EMPLOYERS face multiple challenges while managing their businesses. Besides setting up the necessary infrastructure, the quality of manpower plays a key role in the success of an enterprise. The top operating companies in Pakistan, the numbers of which have shrunk substantially over the last 30 to 40 years, employed the best technicians and operators, who were much wanted by petroleum giants, such as Safco and Aramco.

Such workers are mostly committed to their company’s interests in complying with safety policies and fulfilling job responsibilities. Regular attendance plays a crucial role in judging an employee’s commitment to his job and organisation. In progressive companies, there is a provision of two weekly rest days, and between 20 to 25 days of annual leave against the statutory requirement of 14 days per annum. The quantum of other leaves in the law comprises 10 days of casual leave, 16 days of sick leave, and around 15 days of festival-related holidays per year. The total number of leaves and holidays is approximately 165 days, leaving just 200 days of work in a year. Despite this time off, if an employee is absent from work without approval, they should be disciplined.

Excessive absenteeism exists in industrial and commercial undertakings across the world. The most common reason that is given is sickness. Illness can be feigned; no doctor can ascertain whether the absence was in any way related to a disease. Employees also miss work because of social, cultural and economic reasons. Many are absent because the work is either unrewarding and hazardous or stressful. An employee’s grave personal issues, too, can have a negative impact on their attendance.

Other key causes of absenteeism include a heavy workload, long hours, and high-pressure tasks coupled with the expense of commuting. Chronic illness, injury, and anxiety make sick leave necessary, as does lack of childcare or eldercare. Workers who feel unappreciated or disconnected from company goals are too discouraged to show up, while bullying and lack of support from supervisors make the workplace unsafe.
Employers should identify the causes of absenteeism.

Chronic absenteeism is the consistent absence of an employee from the workplace. This prevents them from carrying out their duties in a timely and productive fashion, which violates a company’s personal or sick leave policy. The hidden costs of absenteeism include overtime for those who cover for absent employees, temporary hiring costs, and the low morale or reduced productivity of those who have to work harder for someone chronically absent. Meanwhile, when such absentees return to the office, they spend the first few days in either catching up, or attending to pending work.

According to Standing Order 15 of the Industrial and Commercial Employment (Standing Orders) Ordinance, 1968, “habitual absence without leave or absence without leave for more than ten days” constitutes misconduct. An employee guilty of misconduct may be dismissed from employment if the charge against him is proven in the domestic inquiry held to investigate the allegation.

However, employers are often advised to proceed against errant employees gradually. The former should first explore the causes of an employee’s absenteeism and, if possible, try to correct inconvenient factors within their organisations. If such an exercise alleviates the absenteeism of an employee, counselling sessions can then be instituted to address stress and anxiety for all. The result will not only be improved overall attendance but also a content and productive workforce. Introducing incentive schemes for employees who maintain an exemplary attendance record also goes a long way in encou­raging people to be present in the office.

In the case of an employee becoming entangled in a criminal case and imprisoned for an unspecified period, the superior courts maintain that it is unfair to expect an employer to keep a post vacant indefinitely.
In all such cases, the employers had invoked the provisions of Standing Order 12 (3) of the Industrial and Commercial Employment (Standing Orders) Ordi-nance, 1968.
It provides that the services of a workman may be terminated by an order in writing, which shall explicitly state the reason for the action taken and is paid one month’s wages in lieu of notice.

In its judgement on April 26, 2021, the Supreme Court of Pakistan agreed with all the judgments of the lower courts, in which the employers had resorted to the aforementioned Standing Order to terminate the services of employees absent for an indefinite period. The SC also held that the services of an employee may be terminated if he is unable to return to work for a period of two months.
The writer is a human resources consultant at the Aga Khan University Hospital.
Published in Dawn, November 24th, 2026

cards.title: The mote in whose eye?
cards.author: Jawed Naqvi
cards.why: This piece is essential for comprehending the historical evolution of Indian politics, the rise of religious nationalism, and its implications for regional dynamics.
cards.summary: Sonia Gandhi's memoir reveals her fears about the aggressive, right-wing forces using religion in Indian politics. The author traces this back to Jawaharlal Nehru's early concerns about Hindu extremists. Indira Gandhi tried to maintain secularism but faced challenges, including the 1975 emergency. Rajiv Gandhi, despite his progressive image, inadvertently deepened religious divisions through actions like appeasing both Muslim reactionaries and Hindu right-wing groups, paving the way for Hindutva's rise.
key_facts: Sonia Gandhi's memoir expresses concern over the 'ruthless and unprincipled' adversary using religion in politics.
Jawaharlal Nehru warned against Hindu extremists as potential destroyers of secular democracy.
Indira Gandhi's tenure from 1966-77 saw her trying to uphold Nehru's secular focus.
The 1975 emergency soiled Indira Gandhi's progressive credentials.
Hindutva gained camouflaged entry into mainstream politics in 1977.
Rajiv Gandhi's actions in the Shahbano alimony case and Babri Masjid dispute deepened religious divides.

vocab.meaning: a natural tendency to behave in a particular way
a tendency to choose or do something regularly; an inclination

text: TERRIFIED by Rahul and Priyanka’s exposure to lurking harm as the siblings negotiate the remorseless world of Indian politics, Sonia Gandhi asks herself sagely in her memoir: “Is it because I understand even more clearly and only too well what is at stake, and the extent to which our adversary is ruthless and unprincipled? Our opponents have always used the garb of religion to further a regressive, right-wing agenda — only now, as their ideology has gained traction, they have become more hardened and violent.”

In describing the right wing’s propensity for violence as a dominant threat to democracy (and to her children), Gandhi reveals an ideological connect with Jawaharlal Nehru. It was Nehru who, soon after independence, would tell his advisers to worry about Hindu extremists rather than communists (who the advisers preferred to target) as the potential destroyers of his idea of secular democracy.
Nehru’s ideas were carried forward by Indira Gandhi in her 1966-77 tenure. She was supported in the task by moderate communists. But she soiled her progressive credentials with the 1975 emergency.

The second tenure in 1980 saw her losing the left’s support and it became an uphill toil for Indira to preserve Nehru’s secular focus while Hindutva, emboldened by its camouflaged 1977 entry into mainstream politics, chipped away at the pillars of secular India, hollowing them out eventually. Rajiv Gandhi saw religion as the flavour of his time. Thus, a man not known for any regressive proclivities plunged headlong into the religious mire he would unwittingly deepen. By siding with Muslim reactionaries in the Shahbano alimony case, he found himself needing to balance the huge political error by appeasing right-wing Hindus in the Babri Masjid dispute. Clearly his advisers were up to no good and several of them proved it by crossing over to the BJP.
Rahul Gandhi can be vividly stern with the right wing at home while favouring a gentler diplomatic vocabulary for outrages abroad.

The ideological focus was blurred further by Manmohan Singh, who put Nehru’s worldview in the loft and asserted instead that the biggest internal threat to the country came from the hard-line left, not, as Nehru had warned, from the Hindu right. Singh was regurgitating the traditionally anti-left propaganda of big businesses. They backed his vertical ascent and used the time to prepare the grounds for Narendra Modi’s arrival. By the time Singh woke up and described Modi as a disaster for India, it was too late. His secular legacy was to have produced the Justice Sachar report about the miserable state Muslims live in, which nobody today wants to talk about.

As for Rahul Gandhi, for reasons best known to him, his fulminations in the US last week detracted from his mother’s calling out the mass murder in Gaza as a genocide that India needed to oppose as its moral tenet. Sonia Gandhi stood out as a rare Indian leader to champion Palestinian rights in Modi’s India. She slammed the government in an opinion piece in a major daily for humouring Israel with its loud diplomatic silence on Gaza. Like her mother, Priyanka too described the genocide as genocide. Rahul hesitantly uses the word to describe Gaza’s nightmare but he is not averse to calling it out as genocide.

He offered a tame response instead to students in New York, reportedly saying one wrong could not be justified by another wrong, the reference being to Hamas as the trigger. In a world polarised by Israeli atrocities, Rahul thus embroiled himself in the notorious action-reaction trope used by right-wing groups mostly to justify targeting weaker quarries.

It is of course possible that being leader of the opposition in the Lok Sabha requires Rahul to be less strident on the diplomatic circuit than his mother or sister are able to be. There’s another likelier reason to be circumspect — the need to keep the US close. It has been suggested that since India’s diplomatic ties with Israel were established in January 1992 within months of Rajiv Gandhi’s assassination, he was somehow the impediment. What is less known is that while Rajiv maintained a formal non-alignment and pro-Palestinian posture, he did take incremental steps towards engagement with Israel. A significant example was that an Israeli tennis team was allowed to tour India in 1987.

Rajiv also yielded to American Jewish leaders ostensibly to get more traction for India in Washington. It resulted in the elevation of the Israeli vice-consul in Bombay to the rank of consul, followed by indirect contacts in Washington and New York in 1988. But despite the limited outreach, he continued to publicly criticise Israeli policies — such as condemning the 1985 attack on PLO offices in Tunis — and maintained support for Palestinian rights. That could be a key difference between Rahul Gandhi and his parents. What makes it curious is that he can be vividly stern with the right-wing establishment at home while favouring a gentler diplomatic vocabulary for outrages abroad.

Rahul’s father, like him, also lived in tricky times. A standoff with China in Arunachal Pradesh melted into a handshake with Deng Xiaoping. Ties with Pakistan soured over India’s military exercise close to its border, which Islamabad saw as a cover for invasion. Rajiv Gandhi dissolved the tensions by holding a memorable meeting with Benazir Bhutto in Karachi. Relations soured with the king of Nepal, Sinhala nationalists as well as Sri Lanka’s Tamil separatists. Rajiv helped create Saarc in 1985 to thrash out the differences. Modi has shut that option.

Finally, a Pakistani student at the US event asked Rahul how ties could improve between the neighbours. Rahul could have recalled how he and Priyanka watched a cricket match in Karachi in 2004 while the two countries discussed terrorism. Why aren’t those India-Pakistan matches played any longer? Rahul could have said that the IRA was furiously attacking British targets, keeping the Good Friday Agreement on the anvil for years. His idea of ‘talks only after terrorism ends’ sounds like Modi’s foreign ministry statement. Or, perhaps it shows the right wing in Congress is alive and kicking, perhaps to Sonia Gandhi’s chagrin.
The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.

cards.title: Delaying the inevitable
cards.author: Arifa Noor
cards.why: This piece offers insights into current political dynamics, inter-party relations, and key constitutional issues in Pakistan.
cards.summary: The Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) is highly concerned about the talk of new provinces, unlike other government parties. Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari recently made strong statements, questioning reserved seats, judicial independence, and the 27th Amendment, and calling for engagement with Imran Khan. This led to a swift backlash from federal ministers. Later, BBZ appeared to soften his stance, suggesting the PPP might be accepting the current political realities.
key_facts: The PPP is reportedly the only government party openly concerned about new provinces discussions.
Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari delivered a significant speech at the Karachi Press Club.
He questioned the award of reserved seats of PTI to other parties.
He alleged the 27th Amendment had been passed by force.
Federal Information Minister Atta Tarar publicly criticized Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari's statements.

vocab.meaning: showing strong feeling; forceful or passionate
well-known, especially so as to be stereotypical
a strong negative reaction by a large number of people

text: THE PPP is worried, very worried. Since the talk of the new provinces began, it has been the only party (in government) to take the ‘rumours’ seriously, in public as well as otherwise; the Noonies would rather ignore the matter. It struck back with vehement rejections and heated speeches in Sindh.

And then last week, Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari took the proverbial bull by the horns. At a speech at the Karachi Press Club, not only did he push back against the idea of new provinces, he also created shock and awe by what he said on other issues. He questioned the award of the reserved seats of PTI to other parties; he expressed concern over the state of the judiciary and even alleged the 27th Amendment had been passed by force. He then also called Imran Khan a political prisoner and said both the PTI head and Maulana Fazlur Rehman needed to be wooed rather than pushed away.

The speech did not go down well, it seems. Within minutes, Atta Tarar, the information minister of the federal government that is yet to own the new provinces officially was on television , to criticise BBZ. Others followed suit, though neither the prime minister nor anyone from the Sharif family spoke up. And no one was willing to spare BBZ.

The next day came a number of interviews in which it seemed at times that the PPP chairman was walking back on his earlier harshness. For instance, when asked to explain his comments on the 27th Amendment, BBZ argued that he meant it was passed by brute majority of the government. Then he called Mohsin Naqvi ‘bhai’ after having described him as the minister of everything a day before.
Some feel the PPP, since the meeting with the president, has accepted the inevitable.

But the explanations didn’t prove enough; soon came the news that the prime minister and interior minister met Asif Ali Zardari, the president, and the press release after their interaction said that any future amendments would be passed with consensus as had happened in the past. Released by the presidency, this press release provided a stamp of legitimacy to the 26th and 27th Amendments, and a contradiction of what BBZ had said.

This is not the first time it has appeared to outsiders that BBZ has been put in his place by his father, but the frequency with which this happens is now more a case of the father and son playing good cop/bad cop as have the Sharif brothers for decades. That it ends up making the son seem mercurial doesn’t seem to bother the party.

Since then, the war of words between the government and the PPP has dialled down a wee bit on television, but on social media, it continues unabated. And the culprits are not just the anonymous accounts. A senior cabinet member such as Khawaja Asif has posted provocatively on X, leading to angry reactions from senior PPP leaders.
However, the ceasefire hasn’t put an end to the larger ‘debate’ on new provinces. And neither has it really clarified the position of the parties in power on the matter.

For instance, some feel the PPP, since the meeting with the president, has now, like the N, accepted the inevitable. After all, no one thinks the N in Lahore is too happy with the idea but it realises the futility of pushing back. This is lent credence by the statements of Rana Sanaullah, who continues to insist the proposal has not been discussed by the government. But it is perhaps too simple to assume an easy capitulation despite what the country continues to be ‘told’.

Journalists with sources and contacts in the highest echelons of power continue to inform us that new provinces are as real as climate change. With their access to the hallowed halls of power, they are privy to some information on how the provinces may go forward, despite the resistance from the PPP.

The first step is a referendum. That Atta Tarar defended this idea in his video talk that followed BBZ’s press conference means there is some truth to the matter; since then Rana Sana has also agreed that a referendum might be the way forward.

In addition, a story in The News has also explained the referendum votes will not be counted nationally but provincially. The Constitution also allows parliament to lay down the procedure “for the holding of a referendum and the compiling and the consolidation of the result of a referendum” in Article 48.

Obviously, some Doubting Thomases continue to point out that a referendum cannot override the need for the provincial assemblies to pass a resolution in favour of new provinces with a two-thirds majority. And while it continues to be a hurdle, some experts, such as Malik Ahmed Khan, the Punjab Assembly speaker, are of the view that once the people have spoken, it should be given more weight than the voice of the representatives of the people. Perhaps he knows how this will translate legally and constitutionally, but it does seem to suggest that the hurdles have been or are being worked out.

But this is what one side is telling us at a time when hybridity afflicts us. And the parties’ disquiet is not entirely hidden. The PPP is more vocal but the N remains coy. And till they are on board the hybrid train, they will have a say. In parliament, in creating a consensus and so on.

It seems that at the moment, their instinct might be to stretch the process out by debating the finer points of the question and how it will be conducted. Consider that in a recent speech BBZ emphasised the need to focus on the economy instead of creating new problems. Beyond that, can this issue strike another blow to the hybrid system? Most probably.
The writer is a journalist.
Published in Dawn, November 24th, 2026
